tldr: To learn robot action representations from vast unlabeled videos, the authors propose "O²LaF," a self-supervised learning framework that repurposes a single pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) into both an inverse dynamics model (estimating actions) and a forward dynamics model (predicting outcomes). In camera navigation and robotic manipulation, it vastly outperforms prior methods in few-shot action probing accuracy and demonstrates zero-shot action transfer from humans to robots.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed O²LaF. An inverse dynamics model (IDM) and a forward dynamics model (FDM), both initialized from the same pretrained video DiT, are optimized end-to-end through a 32-dimensional continuous latent action bottleneck. The IDM functions as a feed-forward extractor using learnable action queries, while the FDM acts as a causal joint predictor under high noise.
overview:
Web videos contain massive amounts of information about how the world changes, but they lack action labels showing what caused those changes. Latent action learning has therefore drawn significant interest as a way to autonomously acquire "action" representations from unlabeled video. Latent action learning typically pairs an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that estimates actions from consecutive video frames with a forward dynamics model (FDM) that predicts the future from those actions. However, prior methods either trained the IDM from scratch or only used video generative models for the FDM, failing to fully leverage the rich spatiotemporal dynamics priors inherent to video models.

The authors asked: "Can a single pretrained video model (video DiT) be repurposed for both the IDM and FDM?" O²LaF (One Prior, Two Dynamics) realizes this idea. Starting from the exact same video DiT, the IDM is adapted into a single-pass action query encoder, while the FDM is independently adapted into a causal generative model for future prediction. To prevent "shortcuts" where the model simply copies previous frames to guess the future, the authors meticulously designed information access controls, including causal joint prediction and training in the high-noise regime.

Evaluations were conducted across two domains: camera navigation (MIND) and real-world robotic manipulation (GR-1). O²LaF not only set a new state of the art in action probing accuracy via linear probing, but also succeeded in zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer, driving a robot using latent actions extracted from human video. This study clearly demonstrates that video pretrained models themselves serve as a powerful foundation for action discovery and future prediction.
contributions: Proposed O²LaF, a novel framework that adapts a single pretrained video DiT to both an inverse dynamics model (IDM) for extracting latent actions and a forward dynamics model (FDM) for predicting the future, training them end-to-end.
Systematized design principles to acquire high-quality latent actions by cutting off generative model information shortcuts, such as causal joint prediction and high-noise sampling in the FDM.

Achieved SOTA linear probing performance in both camera navigation and bimanual robot manipulation, demonstrating zero-shot action transfer from humans to robots and its effectiveness as a video world model.

sections.heading: Tackling the "Plenty of Videos, No Actions" Problem with a Single Video DiT
sections.summary: Because large-scale video data lacks action labels, it is difficult to use directly for training world models and robot policies. Existing latent action learning approaches only partially leveraged pretrained models, but this paper addresses the problem with O²LaF, which repurposes a single video DiT for both the IDM and FDM.
sections.details:
Videos overflowing the internet capture physical changes in the world, but they do not record action labels like agent manipulations or camera movements that caused them. Latent action learning is an approach to make up for this lack of supervisory signals.

A latent action model consists of an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that estimates action representations $z_t$ from observed visual transitions, and a forward dynamics model (FDM) that predicts the future taking those actions as input. By imposing an information bottleneck, $z_t$ is forced to compress the essential causes of change (actions).

However, prior research had a major imbalance. Many methods trained the IDM from scratch, falling short of the expressive power of video foundation models. Moreover, even recent methods that used video generation models for the FDM applied standard diffusion training procedures, causing the model to bypass action conditioning and complete videos on its own.

Modern large-scale video Diffusion Transformers (video DiTs) internally model visual temporal changes with extreme precision. The authors recognized that this rich spatiotemporal prior is precisely what both the IDM and FDM need. Guided by the principle of "one prior, two dynamics," they developed O²LaF.

captions.F2: Paradigm comparison of self-supervised latent action learning: (a) training from scratch, (b) training on frozen features, (c) using a video generator only for the FDM, and (d) using video priors as auxiliary losses. In contrast, the proposed method (Ours) repurposes a single video DiT for both the IDM and FDM, training them end-to-end.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Latent Actions and the Trend of Repurposing Video Generative Models
sections.summary: Latent action learning from action-free videos has progressed from pixel reconstruction to feature-space prediction and the introduction of video pretraining. Recently, research repurposing the internal representations of video generation models for perception and policies has surged, and O²LaF pushes this trend forward into the unsupervised discovery of action representations.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Latent Action Learning from Videos
Efforts to turn unlabeled videos into reusable control representations have long been active. Early studies trained the IDM and FDM from scratch on target videos, but suffered from getting bogged down in fine pixel texture reconstruction. To address this, methods shifted prediction targets to pretrained semantic feature spaces like DINO, or introduced video generative models into the FDM. O²LaF answers an orthogonal architectural question: how to leverage video pretrained models to initialize the dynamics themselves.

### 2.2 Repurposing Video DiTs
Pretrained video generative models have been shown to contain internal representations useful not just for video synthesis, but also for spatiotemporal perception tasks like point tracking and geometry estimation. More recently, attempts have emerged to use video generators as robot policy backbones or world models. However, most prior work grounded these models using real robot action labels. O²LaF sets itself apart by repurposing video priors to discover the action space itself in a self-supervised manner from videos with zero action labels.

sections.heading: Inside O²LaF: Closing Information Shortcuts to Surface Latent Actions
sections.summary: Based on the Wan2.2 video DiT, the IDM is adapted as a single-pass action query encoder, and the FDM as a causal joint predictor. By eliminating shortcuts—such as autoregressively copying the previous frame or target leakage at low noise levels—information is forced to concentrate into the action bottleneck.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Preliminaries and Motivation
When prompting a pretrained video DiT (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B) with the text "What is the action in the video?" and visualizing cross-attention, attention naturally concentrated on human manipulating hands and moving object regions. This observation provided strong motivation that video DiTs can be repurposed for action extraction.

### 3.2 Problem Formulation and Architecture
For each transition $x_i \rightarrow x_{i+1}$ in an input video, a 32-dimensional continuous latent action $z_i$ is estimated. The IDM $q_\phi$ and FDM $f_\theta$ are initialized from the same pretrained video DiT and independently adapted using LoRA (rank-128).

### 3.3 Video DiT as Inverse Dynamics (IDM)
The IDM outputs latent actions in a single forward pass without iterative denoising. To extract transition information, learnable "action queries" are introduced. Each query $q_i$ attends only to the two consecutive frames $(x_i, x_{i+1})$ via an asymmetric attention mask, blocking attention between queries as well as backward attention from video tokens. Query outputs pass through a linear Gaussian head to yield 32-dimensional continuous latent actions $z_i$.

### 3.4 Video DiT as Forward Dynamics (FDM)
The FDM jointly predicts future state sequences conditioned on the initial frame $x_0$ and the latent action sequence $\overline{\mathbf{z}}$. Two critical design choices are made here:
- **Causal Joint Prediction**: In autoregressive generation models, the model can predict the future simply by copying the clean previous frame, causing latent actions to be ignored. Therefore, noise is added across all future frames, and velocity is predicted jointly while applying temporal causal attention.
- **Training in High-Noise Regimes**: In intermediate noise regimes, target information leaks from the noisy future frames themselves. Hence, noise levels $t_{\mathrm{FDM}}$ are sampled with emphasis on high-noise regions (near 1), forcing the model to reconstruct the future relying strictly on the initial state and actions.

### 3.5 End-to-End Optimization
Clean frames ($t_{\mathrm{IDM}}=0$) are fed to the IDM, while $t_{\mathrm{FDM}}$ sampled from a high-noise distribution is provided to the FDM. Using the sum of Flow Matching loss and latent space KL regularization ($\beta=10^{-4}$), prediction error gradients from the FDM flow through the action bottleneck to the IDM for end-to-end optimization.

sections.heading: Experimental Results: Higher Probing Accuracy and Zero-Shot Action Transfer
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted on camera navigation (MIND) and real robot manipulation (GR-1). O²LaF significantly outperformed prior methods in few-shot action probing and demonstrated zero-shot action transfer from human first-person video to robot motions both qualitatively and quantitatively.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
- **Camera Navigation**: Self-supervised training on MiraData, evaluated on the MIND benchmark. Evaluates exact-match accuracy across 4 simultaneous ternary axes: forward/backward, left/right, up/down, and rotation.
- **Robot Manipulation**: Trained strictly on EgoDex (human everyday manipulation egocentric videos) and evaluated on the GR-1 physical robot benchmark (DreamDojo In-lab Eval). Measures the coefficient of determination $R^2$ for bimanual end-effector (EEF) positions and orientations.

### 4.2 Latent Action Quality (Few-Shot Probing)
Linear probes were trained on few labeled data with the latent action encoder frozen. In GR-1 robot manipulation, O²LaF's accuracy surged rapidly with just a few episodes, ultimately reaching $R^2 = 0.277$. This vastly outperforms DreamDojo's $0.149$, which was trained on large-scale datasets of both humans and robots—O²LaF nearly doubled the score while trained only on human video. This shows that the latent actions capture essential motion structures across different embodiments.

### 4.3 Zero-Shot Action Transfer
Latent action sequences extracted from one video were applied to completely different initial frames to generate videos.
- **Camera Navigation**: Both first-person and third-person viewpoints faithfully reproduced target camera movements and agent rotations. Furthermore, applying Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG=3) on latent actions further improved trajectory errors (NRMSE and RPE).
- **Cross-Embodiment Manipulation**: Extracting actions from a video of a human reaching and grasping an object and applying them to a static robot image resulted in generated videos where the robot arm accurately reached toward the object. In human $\rightarrow$ robot $\rightarrow$ human cycle-reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS), it consistently outperformed DreamDojo.

captions.F7: Generation results of zero-shot transfer in camera navigation. Camera and agent motions from the reference video (top row) are accurately reproduced in a completely different target scene (bottom row).
captions.F8: Zero-shot cross-embodiment transfer between human and robot. Latent actions extracted from human reaching motions seamlessly transfer to accurate reaching motions by a robot arm.

sections.heading: Ablation Studies: Why Does This Design Work?
sections.summary: Systematic analyses were conducted on IDM/FDM noise design, temporal causality, and backbone choices. While self-supervised representations like V-JEPA2 yield high probing accuracy, visual appearance (e.g., color) leaks into actions; sharing video DiT priors proved optimal for generative transfer.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Adaptation and Scaling of Pretrained Dynamics
Freezing the video DiT weights and training only the action queries resulted in a substantial performance drop, proving that LoRA adaptation is indispensable. In addition, scaling up FDM parameters from 1.3B to 14B while keeping the IDM size fixed consistently improved the quality of actions acquired by the IDM. This confirms that stronger prediction capability boosts action extraction quality.

### 5.2 Information Access Control and Noise Design
A $5\times 5$ grid comprehensively investigated noise levels $(t_{\mathrm{IDM}}, t_{\mathrm{FDM}})$ for the IDM and FDM. Low FDM noise causes target cheating, sharply degrading performance. Conversely, adding a moderate amount of noise to the IDM ($t_{\mathrm{IDM}} \approx 0.3$) tended to improve accuracy, as fine textures are removed, allowing the model to focus on abstract motion information.

### 5.3 Comparison with Other Pretrained Representations
V-JEPA2 (self-supervised predictive representations) and VideoChat3 (video-language model) were examined as IDM backbones. Interestingly, V-JEPA2 recorded the highest numerical linear probing score. However, when using V-JEPA2 latent actions to generate videos of different scenes, "appearance leakage" occurred prominently, where background and object colors from the source video bled into the target. V-JEPA2 also showed high leakage in color probing (Color $R^2$). High probing accuracy does not equate to a clean, transferable action space; pairing video DiTs proved to have the best appearance preservation and controllability.

captions.F9: Grid search results of IDM and FDM noise levels (flow times). When FDM noise is low, action estimation accuracy drops significantly, confirming that high noise is crucial for enforcing action dependence.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Video Generation Models as Engines for Action Discovery
sections.summary: By repurposing video DiT priors for both the IDM and FDM, O²LaF enables high-quality latent action learning from unlabeled videos. It demonstrates that video foundation models can go beyond mere content generation to become general-purpose dynamics foundations for discovering and predicting control representations in the physical world.
sections.details:
Focusing on the powerful spatiotemporal modeling capabilities of video DiTs, this work proposed a framework that instantiates two paired dynamics—action estimation and outcome prediction—from a single prior. By strictly controlling information flow, it showed that control representations transferable across embodiments and environments can be extracted even from unlabeled videos.

Future work includes improving the interpretability of the acquired latent action space and applying it to real-world closed-loop control and fast trajectory planning.

sections.heading: Appendix: Action Query Attention and Application to Robot Verification
sections.summary: Visualizations confirmed that learned action queries attend locally to hands and manipulated objects that are key to transitions. Furthermore, an application is demonstrated where the FDM serves as a "Policy Verifier" to bridge the sim-to-real gap.
sections.details:
### Attention Visualization of Action Queries
When the IDM extracts actions from transitions $x_i \rightarrow x_{i+1}$, visualizations showed where action queries attend among spatial tokens. The queries focused strongly on moving agents, manipulated objects, and contact points of end-effectors (human hands or robot grippers), confirming that they locally capture physical change cues.

### Policy Verification via FDM (Policy Verifier)
An application of using the FDM as a safety check before deploying AI-generated robot code or policies to real hardware is presented. When building and running a MuJoCo simulator from a single photograph, grasping can fail due to errors from simplified mesh geometries. Because the FDM can roll out real-world physical behavior from real photographs with high fidelity, it can detect discrepancies between simulation results and FDM predictions, serving as a verifier that detects failure risks prior to physical deployment.

captions.F11: Visualization of regions attended by action queries. Across navigation, human manipulation, and robot manipulation, attention consistently concentrates on moving vehicles, hands, robot arms, and grasped objects.

takeaways: Video DiTs serve not only for video generation, but also as an exceptional initialization for inverse dynamics models that extract latent actions in a single forward pass.

When using generative models for forward dynamics (FDM) in latent action learning, causal joint prediction (to prevent copying previous frames) and high-noise sampling (to prevent target leakage) are essential.

High probing accuracy alone should not be used to judge latent action quality. Models like V-JEPA2 can score high on probing while leaking appearance information, making downstream generative transfer evaluation critical.
limitations: It remains difficult to directly interpret the internal structure of the acquired 32-dimensional continuous latent action space, such as which specific physical parameters it maps to.
Video diffusion models incur high computational costs, making them difficult to deploy as-is for real-time closed-loop control or fast Model Predictive Control (MPC) rollouts on physical robots.
Performance depends on the diversity of viewpoints and motions in the training dataset, creating a trade-off in the balancing ratio between domain-specific and general-purpose data.
